p.t: Over the past two decades, researchers have documented a number of new facts about the credit cycle. High credit growth is associated with both a higher probability of a future financial crisis and lower future GDP growth (Schularick and Taylor, 2012;López-Salido, Stein, and Zakrajšek, 2017;Mian, Sufi, and Verner, 2017). Credit market returns are also predictable, suggesting a role for investor sentiment in the credit cycle. Greenwood and Hanson (2013) document that periods of elevated corporate credit growth and low average borrower credit quality forecast low returns to credit. In a large panel of countries, Baron and Xiong (2017) find that high bank credit growth forecasts low returns to bank stocks. Moreover, Greenwood, Hanson, Shleifer, and Sørensen (2022) show that the combination of large credit expansions and asset price booms predicts financial crises. A recurring theme in discussions of the credit cycle is that, at short horizons, credit market dynamics can be fairly disconnected from contemporaneous movements in the stock market or the broader macroeconomy. In post-war U.S. history, credit expansions and contractions have often followed a similar pattern: credit grows slowly as the economy emerges from a recession, accelerates during the expansion, and in some episodes continues to expand even as aggregate economic growth begins to slow. For example, in the upswing preceding the 2008 financial crisis, GDP growth peaked in March 2005, while credit growth peaked nearly two years later, in March 2007, a period when credit spreads were near historical lows. These patterns suggest that, over short horizons, credit conditions may evolve differently from standard business-cycle indicators. However, many influential models of the credit cycle-e.g., Bernanke and Gertler (1989), Holmström and Tirole (1997), Bernanke, Gertler, and Gilchrist (1999), and even more recent behavioral models such as Bordalo, Gennaioli, and Shleifer (2018)-feature a single state variable, so that credit frictions or belief distortions primarily amplify business-cycle fluctuations rather than generating distinct credit-cycle dynamics.

In this paper, we present a new behavioral model of the credit cycle that is consistent with much of the accumulating evidence on credit cycles, but also speaks to periods of disconnect between credit markets and economic fundamentals. A key feature of our model is "reflexivity," the idea that there is a dynamic two-way feedback loop between investors' biased beliefs and market outcomes. In finance, the idea of reflexivity is most prominently associated with the investor George Soros, who argued that "distorted views can influence the situation to which they relate because false views lead to inappropriate actions" (Financial Times, October 26, 2009). 1 In credit markets, reflexivity arises because investors who overestimate the creditworthiness of a borrower refinance maturing debt on more favorable terms, thereby making the borrower less likely to default, at least in the short run. In the long run, such a borrower may take on additional leverage, ultimately becoming more vulnerable to default. Our model builds on prior dynamic models of firm capital structure, including Leland (1994), He and Xiong (2012), and DeMarzo and He (2021), by adding a behavioral component. In our model, debt financing is provided by a set of biased bond investors whose beliefs about the likelihood of future firm defaults depend only on the firm's recent default history. Following periods of low defaults, these bond investors-who are "default extrapolators"-believe that debt is safe and hence refinance maturing debt on attractive terms. We study the interaction between these behavioral bond investors and a representative rational firm who maximizes its equity value, thus adopting the "rational managers with irrational investors" approach to behavioral corporate finance. 2 The core assumption in this literature and in our paper, which is supported by the evidence reviewed below, is that firm managers can detect and respond to market mispricing. 3 Specifically, the rational firm exploits bond investor sentiment by optimally issuing more (less) debt when bond investors are overly optimistic (pessimistic) about the likelihood of future defaults. The firm also optimally chooses when to default and this decision depends on the level of bond investor sentiment. 4 Because bond investors hold extrapolative beliefs based on defaults-which are endogenously determined in the model-rather than on the firm's exogenous fundamentals, a dynamic feedback loop arises between biased investor beliefs and firm defaults. Current investor beliefs affect future defaults through the terms on which investors are willing to refinance debt today. 5 Figure 1 illustrates this two-way feedback loop.

During a credit boom, default rates are low, leading bond investors to believe that future default rates will continue to be low. In the near term, these optimistic beliefs tend to be partially selffulfilling. Holding constant the firm's cash flow fundamentals, the perception of low future default risk raises bond prices. The availability of cheap debt financing makes it attractive for the firm to continue refinancing its maturing debt-even in situations where a deterioration in fundamentals would otherwise lead the firm to exercise its default option-thereby reducing the true likelihood of a near-term default. Over longer horizons, however, the optimistic beliefs that prevail during credit booms tend to be self-defeating. When bond investors are overly optimistic, the firm optimally increases leverage to take advantage of cheap debt financing. As a result, optimistic beliefs about default risk lead to an endogenous buildup of financial fragility, which raises the true likelihood of a default in the long run. These two effects imply that a firm with weak fundamentals can frequently skate by for some time when investors are bullish, a phenomenon that we refer to as the "calm before the storm." However, these bullish investor beliefs lead to a predictable rise in firm leverage and an endogenous buildup of fragility. Eventually, the firm will be hit by an unexpected adverse shock to cash flow fundamentals that, when combined with the prior rise in firm leverage, triggers a default. Conversely, suppose that the economy has just experienced an initial default and enters a credit bust. Because investors over-extrapolate recent outcomes, they come to believe that the likelihood of future defaults is high-even if the firm restructures and reduces its leverage following the default.

In the short run, these bearish beliefs are again partially self-fulfilling: by making it more costly for the firm to refinance maturing debt, they induce the firm to lower the leverage threshold at which it defaults, thereby increasing the true probability of default in the near term. Over longer horizons, however, these bearish beliefs tend to be self-defeating. When debt financing is expensive, the firm optimally chooses to delever, thereby improving its balance sheet and reducing future default risk. In some circumstances, our model generates "default spirals," in which an initial default triggers an extended sequence of subsequent defaults, much like the episodes observed in sovereign debt restructurings (Das, Papaioannou, and Trebesch, 2012). The economy's vulnerability to such default spirals depends not only on investor beliefs but also on the firm's pre-default balance sheet. Intuitively, default spirals are more likely following a prolonged calm period during which the firm has accumulated substantial leverage. In that case, multiple rounds of default and restructuring may be required for the firm to sufficiently delever. In our model, transitions between credit booms and credit busts are ultimately caused by changes in the firm's cash flow fundamentals. However, because investors extrapolate past defaults and not cash flow fundamentals, these transitions are not fully synchronized with changes in fundamentals and can be highly path-dependent. For example, our model generates "calm before the storm" periods in which the cash flow fundamentals of the economy have turned, but credit markets are still buoyant. These episodes are consistent with Krishnamurthy and Muir (2025), who show that credit spreads are typically too low in the years preceding financial crises.

What happens if bond investors exogenously become more optimistic, revising down their perceived likelihood of future defaults? We show that such a shock to beliefs can be self-fulfilling in our model. Rising investor optimism means that the firm can issue debt at more attractive credit spreads. As a result, the firm optimally delays default, leading investors to become even more optimistic and further reducing credit spreads. This mechanism may help make sense of the 2020-2021 period in U.S. credit markets, where improvements in investor sentiment may have helped save the economy from a wave of defaults stemming from poor fundamentals, as argued by Hanson, Stein, Sunderam, and Zwick (2020). There is a limit on the extent to which investor optimism can be self-fulfilling, however, because under-priced credit eventually induces firms to become highly leveraged, making them more vulnerable to adverse fundamental shocks and thus raising the likelihood of default over longer horizons. Although the feedback loop between biased investor expectations and market outcomes is always present, there are times when it is stronger. We use the model to characterize the conditions under which changes in investors' biased expectations have the most powerful impact on market outcomes. Our model matches many of the empirical facts about credit cycles that researchers have documented in recent years. First, rapid credit growth appears to be a strong predictor of future financial crises and business cycle downturns (Schularick and Taylor, 2012;Mian et al., 2017;López-Salido et al., 2017), a result that is consistent with our model because outstanding credit grows rapidly when sentiment is high but cash flow fundamentals are poor. Relatedly, economies that have experienced high credit growth are more fragile, in the sense that they are more vulnerable to adverse shocks (Krishnamurthy and Muir, 2025). Second, high credit growth predicts low future returns on risky bonds in a univariate forecasting regression (Greenwood and Hanson, 2013;Baron and Xiong, 2017;Muir, 2022), a result that obtains in our model because the firm optimally issues large quantities of debt when investors underestimate the likelihood of future defaults. In our model, credit spreads are typically too low just before the economy experiences a wave of defaults, consistent with the evidence in Krishnamurthy and Muir (2025). Third, when credit markets become highly overheated, our model generates conditional expected excess returns on risky bonds that are significantly negative. This result, which is consistent with prior empirical evidence, is difficult to square with rational, risk-based models of credit cycles and therefore motivates models like ours that prominently feature biased investor beliefs.

After developing the main model, we contrast our findings with those of a benchmark rational model, in which both equity and debt investors are fully rational and forward-looking. In this rational model, deteriorating firm fundamentals cause forward-looking bond investors to perceive a higher likelihood of future firm defaults, leading bond prices to fall and credit spreads to rise. Conversely, following a default, the post-restructuring decline in firm leverage appropriately makes rational bond investors less concerned about the prospect of default, reducing the likelihood of another default in the near future. In other words, this fully rational model does not generate the "calm before the storm" and "default spiral" phenomena captured by our behavioral model. Moreover, by construction, bond returns are not predictable in this model. Finally, we discuss a key difference between our model and an alternative behavioral model that features a rational firm and a set of behavioral bond investors who extrapolate the firm's past fundamental growth (rather than past defaults). Consider a situation in which the firm's fundamentals have been deteriorating, but no default has yet occurred. In our baseline model, the firm optimally delays default because overly optimistic bond investors keep the cost of debt issuance low. By contrast, in the alternative model where investors extrapolate from past fundamentals, the firm optimally lowers the leverage threshold at which it defaults-this tends to accelerate defaultbecause overly pessimistic bond investors make it more costly for the firm to issue debt.

Our paper has much in common with Austrian theories of the credit cycle, including Mises (1924) and Hayek (1925), as well as the accounts of booms, panics, and crashes in Minsky (1986) and Kindleberger (1978). More recently, the idea that investors may neglect tail risk in credit markets was developed theoretically by Greenwood and Hanson (2013), Gennaioli, Shleifer, and Vishny (2012, 2015), and Bordalo et al. (2018). We also draw on growing evidence that investors extrapolate cash flows, past returns, or past crash occurrences (Barberis, Shleifer, and Vishny, 1998;Greenwood and Shleifer, 2014;Barberis, Greenwood, Jin, andShleifer, 2015, 2018;Jin, 2015;Greenwood and Hanson, 2015). Most related here is Jin (2015), who develops a model in which investors' perceptions of crash risk depend on recent experience. Bordalo et al. (2018) present a model of credit cycles in which extrapolative investor expectations play a central role and bond returns are predictable. While their model is similar to ours in several respects, extrapolative expectations in their framework are perfectly tied to cash flow fundamentals. By contrast, in our model, investor beliefs are tied to endogenous credit market outcomes, allowing fundamentals and beliefs to become disconnected. Also related is Krishnamurthy and Li (2025), who analyze the extent to which a behavioral model of credit cycles-similar to ours-can quantitatively match historical evidence. In Section II, we briefly summarize a number of stylized facts about the credit cycle, drawing on the papers cited above and presenting new observations about the synchronicity of the credit and business cycles. Section III develops a dynamic continuous-time model of the credit market with a rational firm and a set of behavioral bond investors who form beliefs about future firm defaults by extrapolating past defaults. We explain the two-way feedback mechanism that is at the heart of our model. In Section IV, we formally define reflexivity and analyze its properties.

We discuss how the model matches a number of features of credit cycles documented in recent years, including the predictability of bond returns and low credit spreads before crises. Section V contrasts our framework with two other models: a fully rational model with forward-looking bond investors and an alternative behavioral model in which bond investors extrapolate recent growth in firm fundamentals. Section VI concludes.

p.s: II. Motivating facts about the credit cycle
p.t: We begin by summarizing a set of stylized facts about credit cycles. The first four facts are drawn from prior work, but we show that they continue to hold using more recent data; the fifth is based on new empirical analysis of our own. Observation 1. Rapid credit growth predicts financial crises and business cycle downturns. In a panel of 14 countries dating back to 1870, Schularick and Taylor (2012) show that rapid credit growth predicts financial crises and interpret their evidence as suggesting that financial crises are episodes of "credit booms gone bust. " Mian et al. (2017) show that rapid credit growthespecially growth in household credit-predicts future declines in GDP growth in an panel of 30 countries from 1960 to 2012. Similarly, López-Salido et al. (2017) show that frothy credit market conditions-proxied by declines in the credit quality of corporate borrowers and by low credit spreads-predict low GDP growth in U.S. data from 1929 to 2015. López-Salido et al. (2017) attribute their findings to predictable reversals in credit market sentiment. Using an international panel of 38 countries, Kirti (2025) shows that rapid credit growth accompanied by a deterioration in lending standards-i.e., declining borrower credit quality-is associated with low future GDP growth. Relatedly, Greenwood et al. (2022) show that the probability of a future crisis is particularly elevated when rapid credit growth is accompanied by a boom in asset prices.

p.s: II. Motivating facts about the credit cycle
p.t: A corollary of Observation 1 is that economies that have experienced high credit growth are more fragile. Krishnamurthy and Muir (2025) argue that a natural interpretation of the findings in Schularick and Taylor (2012) is that rapid credit growth creates financial fragility. When a more leveraged economy is exogenously hit by a negative fundamental shock, such as a large decline in house prices, this results in a financial crisis. Alternately, crises may be triggered by predictable reversals in credit market sentiment, as argued by López-Salido et al. (2017). Consistent with this view, Krishnamurthy and Muir (2025) show that credit spreads are typically "too low" in the years preceding financial crises. The model we develop reflects these ideas: credit booms feature low credit spreads, rapid credit growth, an endogenous rise in firm leverage, and a buildup of financial fragility. Observation 2. Credit market overheating-signaled either by (i) rapid growth in debt outstanding or by (ii) a decline in the credit quality of debt issuers set against the backdrop of relatively low credit spreads-predicts low future returns on risky bonds. Observation 4. Episodes of credit market overheating tend to follow periods of tranquility in credit markets, namely periods when defaults are low and when the returns on risky bonds are high. This suggests that credit market investors extrapolate from past defaults. What outcomes are credit market investors over-extrapolating? One view is that investors overextrapolate an underlying set of economic fundamentals-e.g., firm cash flows or the state of broader macroeconomy. This view leads to behavioral versions of the q-theory of investment (Greenwood and Hanson, 2015;Gennaioli, Ma, and Shleifer, 2016;Bordalo et al., 2018). An alternative view, however, is that credit market investors tend to over-extrapolate recent credit market outcomes. Consistent with this view, Greenwood and Hanson (2013) show that past defaults and credit returns play a dominant role in shaping credit market sentiment. They find that debt issuer quality tends to deteriorate following periods with low realized corporate defaults and high realized returns on risky corporate bonds. p.s: III. A model of credit market sentiment
p.t: In this section, we develop a behavioral model of the credit cycle. The model has two key features. First, corporate bond investors form beliefs about the likelihood of future firm defaults by extrapolating past defaults and set bond prices accordingly. Second, facing these behavioral bond investors, a representative firm maximizes its equity value by choosing how much debt to issue and whether to exercise its option to default. We begin by describing the model setup. We then discuss the model solution and make several observations about the model's key properties. We provide a detailed discussion of the model's implications in Section IV.

Model setup. The model setup follows DeMarzo and He (2021) and is set in continuous time. We consider a representative firm that generates a pretax operating cash flow of δV t at time t. We refer to V t as the firm's fundamental and assume it follows a geometric Brownian motion: where µ > 0 is the average growth rate of the firm's cash flows and ω t is a Brownian motion. All investors are risk neutral and have a constant discount rate of r > µ. 11 We assume a constant corporate tax rate of τ > 0. Thus, the unlevered value of the firm at time t is δ(1 -τ )V t /(r -µ). The firm can issue bonds, and we let F t denote the total face value of outstanding bonds at time t. Bonds have a constant coupon rate of c > 0 and amortize exponentially at rate ξ > 0. Thus, over the period [t, t + dt], bondholders are entitled to coupon payments of cF t dt and principal payments of ξF t dt. If investors thought default were impossible, the bond price (per unit of face value) would be However, default is possible: if equity holders choose not to make these required payments, the firm defaults and bondholders are assumed to recover a fixed fraction η of outstanding principal, where 0 < η < (c + ξ)/(r + ξ).

We assume that firm managers and equity investors are rational. Managers maximize the firm's equity value by choosing the amount of debt to issue and whether to default at each instant. Thus, in the version of our model with rational bond investors, debt issuance and the firm's leverage dynamics reflect dynamic trade-off theory considerations as in DeMarzo and He (2021). Specifically, issuing debt is beneficial because interest payments are tax-deductible, but higher leverage is costly because default entails deadweight costs; the interaction of these two frictions determines the firm's optimal capital structure. However, because we allow bond investors to hold biased beliefs about the likelihood of future defaults, debt can be mispriced, and debt issuance is partially driven by a market-timing motive. All else equal, firms choose to issue more (less) debt when bond investors are overly optimistic (pessimistic) about future default risk.

Motivated by the empirical evidence presented in Section II, we assume that bond investors form beliefs about the likelihood of future firm defaults by extrapolating past defaults. Firm behavior and equity valuation. The firm's managers and equity investors are rational. Managers maximize the firm's equity value by choosing both the amount of debt to issue and whether to default at each instant. Since equity holders receive nothing in default, the value of equity at time t equals the discounted expected value of future net cash flows to equity from time t until the unknown time of default. Our model captures the idea that, in credit markets, there is a dynamic two-way feedback loop between investors' biased beliefs and financial market outcomes. Past defaults affect investors' beliefs about future defaults through equation ( 5). These biased beliefs have two effects. First, they affect bond prices through equation ( 8), which in turn affect the firm's optimal debt issuance through equation ( 12) and its debt accumulation through equation ( 9). Second, biased beliefs lead the firm to optimally adjust its default boundary v b (λ), as shown in Panel A of Figure 5. Together, these two effects allow biased investor beliefs to impact the true probability of future defaults. Specifically, in the short run, such beliefs tend to be partially self-fulfilling and hence self-sustaining. Over longer horizons, however, they can become self-defeating: optimistic investor beliefs eventually lead to an endogenous buildup of leverage and financial fragility that raises the longer-run probability of default. Reflexivity is the idea that there is a dynamic two-way feedback loop between investors' biased beliefs and market outcomes. In this section, we focus on a particular market outcome, namely the true probability that the firm defaults over the next year. We let Pr R (v, λ) denote this true probability of default and provide a formal definition of reflexivity. As before, we discretize our continuous-time model at a monthly frequency. For a given initial state (v, λ), we compute Pr R (v, λ) as follows. We simulate the economy 25,000 times, all starting from this same initial state. Pr R (v, λ) is the fraction of these simulations in which the firm defaults within the next 12 months. With Pr R (v, λ) in hand, we measure the degree of investor bias by comparing this true default probability with investors' perceived probability of observing a default within the next 12 months, which is Pr B (λ) = 1 0 e -λs ds = 1 -e -λ . Here, the superscript "B" denotes the biased expectations of extrapolative investors. We therefore define investors' belief bias as Pr R (v, λ) -Pr B (λ). If this quantity is positive, investor beliefs are overly optimistic; if it is negative, investor beliefs are overly pessimistic. default within 12 months is significantly lower than the true probability. Conversely, for high values of λ, investors are overly pessimistic: their perceived probability of observing a default within 12 months is significantly higher than the true probability. Moreover, for most values of v and λ, Pr R (v, λ) -Pr B (λ) is either significantly positive or significantly negative, indicating that investor beliefs are often biased at any given point in time.

We now study how investors' biased beliefs impact the true probability of future default. We propose ∂ Pr R (v, λ)/∂λ as a formal measure of reflexivity-namely, the sensitivity of the true default probability Pr R (v, λ) with respect to changes in investor beliefs λ. 23 The left panel of Figure 8 shows that ∂ Pr R (v, λ)/∂λ is positive for all values of v and λ: making investors more pessimistic (raising λ) always increases the true probability of a firm default within 12 months. Moreover, ∂ Pr R (v, λ)/∂λ is particularly large for high values of λ and low values of v that are close to the default boundary v b (λ). When investors are highly pessimistic, bond prices are low and the firm sets a high default boundary v b (λ). In this case, reducing λ raises bond prices, leading the firm to lower its optimal default boundary substantially, and, thereby delaying or even preventing future defaults. By contrast, for low values of λ and low values of v near the default boundary v b (λ), ∂ Pr R (v, λ)/∂λ remains positive but is much smaller in magnitude. As we discuss in Sections IV.C and IV.D, this region-characterized by low λ and low v-is associated with heightened financial fragility in credit markets.

p.s: IV.B. The "calm before the storm" phenomenon
p.t: The "calm before the storm" phenomenon also helps make sense of what Gennaioli and Shleifer (2018) have dubbed the "quiet period" of the 2008 global financial crisis-the period between the initial disruptions in housing and credit markets in the summer of 2007 and onset of a full-blown financial crises in the fall of 2008. Specifically, backward-looking default extrapolation helps create a self-fulfilling "quiet period." In our model, the absence of recent defaults leads to a lower λ, which, as Figure 10 shows, tends to further lengthen the calm period. Indeed, as Gennaioli and Shleifer (2018) argue, if investors were fully forward-looking, one should have expected a more rapid deterioration of financial conditions in late 2007 rather than the delayed onset that was witnessed.

Once the first default hits the credit market, default extrapolation can generate a "default spiral": extrapolative, backward-looking beliefs lead to a form of default persistence that is absent when beliefs are fully rational and forward-looking. 24 Specifically, following a default, equation ( 5) implies that investor beliefs become more pessimistic. This pushes down bond prices, increases the cost of debt issuance, and causes the firm to raise its default boundary. As a consequence of the rising default boundary, the firm experiences a series of defaults in rapid succession. Along the way, it gradually delevers and eventually re-enters the no-default region. Figure 9 from Section IV.B provides a numerical example of the "default spiral" phenomenon: in the sample path with (v 0 , λ 0 ) = (0.65, 0.33), the first default hits the credit market at month 39 after a long calm period; it is then followed by four additional consecutive defaults. In this section, we provide further analysis of this phenomenon. We proceed by constructing a measure of the subsequent "default severity" which is the rationally-expected number of firm defaults over the next five years given the current state (v t , λ t ). For each initial state (v t , λ t ), we run 10,000 simulations at a monthly frequency for a length of five years. For each simulation, we compute (Number of defaults) t→t+5 , the number of defaults between month t and month t + 60. We then compute Ψ(v t , λ t ) as the average number of defaults across these 10,000 simulations.

Panel A of Figure 11 presents a heatmap of Ψ(v, λ) for different values of (v, λ). It shows that subsequent default severity is particularly high for low values of λ and low values of v that are near the default boundary v b (λ). In this region, a long calm period in credit markets has led the firm to accumulate significant leverage, making it vulnerable to adverse fundamental shocks. In other words, there has been an endogenous buildup of financial fragility.

p.s: IV.D. The endogenous buildup of fragility during credit booms
p.t: Why does our model of credit cycles feature an endogenous buildup of fragility? During a calm period without defaults, λ declines and bond prices p(λ) rise as investors come to believe that the likelihood of future defaults is low. Meanwhile, so long as firm fundamentals v are not too far from the default boundary v b (λ), the firm will optimally chooses to issue large quantities of debt because bonds prices are high and additional debt is not costly from the perspective of equity holders-i.e., -E F is low. (Recall that Figure 4 shows that g * (v, λ) -ξ is highest when both v and λ are low.) Naturally, this elevated rate of debt issuance raises firm leverage-i.e., v tends to decline. Thus, in the absence of large shocks to firm fundamentals, the economy endogenously drifts toward the region when both λ and v are low-i.e., where credit market sentiment is elevated and firm leverage is high. Moreover, because bond investors are optimistic (low λ), the firm endogenously chooses a low default boundary v b (λ), delaying the arrival of defaults. In the absence of large shocks, this combination of rapid debt issuance and a low default boundary tends to trap v at low values. At the same time, when both λ and v are low, the economy is in a financially fragile state: a large adverse shock will trigger a severe crisis that features a rapid sequence of defaults. (λ, v). In other words, these arrows show how the economy evolves in the absence of shocks to fundamentals. 25 The magnitude of these arrows is larger when the economy is farther from the fragile region (low λ and low v) and becomes smaller as the economy enters this region. As a result, in the absence of large adverse shocks, the economy would spend a long time in this highly fragile region.

The "calm before the storm" and "default spiral" dynamics together highlight the potential disconnect between the endogenous credit cycle and the underlying business cycle that is at the heart of our model. The calm period is partially self-fulfilling in the short run: the absence of recent defaults leads to a lower λ, which allows the firm to lower its default boundary v b (λ) and hence temporarily avoid default even in the face of deteriorating fundamentals. However, because it leads to an endogenous buildup of fragility, elevated credit market sentiment tends to be self-defeating in the long run. Moreover, toward the end of a long calm period, the credit cycle and the business cycle are often not synchronized: firm fundamentals are deteriorating while credit expansion continues.

Our baseline behavioral model in Section III is a model of default extrapolation: bond investors do not directly attend to firm fundamentals; instead, they form beliefs about the firm's creditworthiness by extrapolating past defaults. As emphasized in Section IV, default extrapolation gives rise to both the "calm before the storm" and the "default spiral" phenomena, allowing for a significant disconnect between the credit cycle and the business cycle. It is instructive to contrast our model of default extrapolation with models of fundamental extrapolation models in credit markets such as Bordalo et al. (2018). Specifically, consider an alternative model that features a rational firm and behavioral bond investors who extrapolate the firm's past fundamental growth. A tractable implementation would assume that the true evolution of firm fundamentals follows (3), with a constant growth rate of µ. However, bond investors would incorrectly believe that the growth rate μt is a latent variable that randomly switches between a high value of μt = µ h and a low value μt = µ l < µ h . These bond investors would then use Bayesian inference to compute the expected growth rate µ t = E B t [μ t ] at each point in time t, leading them to incorrectly expect high (low) future fundamental growth when recent realized growth has been high (low).

Almost by construction, such a model would be consistent with some of the evidence on bond return predictability. However, because bond investors extrapolate from the firm's exogenous fundamentals, this alternative model is not "reflexive": it does not feature a dynamic two-way feedback loop between biased investor beliefs and market outcomes. While biased investor beliefs would certainly affect bond prices, debt issuance, and the firm's default decisions, these endogenous market outcomes would not, in turn, affect future biased investor beliefs: the evolution of investor beliefs would depend solely on the exogenous future evolution of fundamentals. As a result, the credit cycle would remain tightly linked with the business cycle-i.e., with the evolution of firm fundamentals. This model would not generate either the "calm before the storm" or the "default spiral" phenomenon. To illustrate, consider a scenario in which the firm's fundamentals have been deteriorating but no default has yet occurred. In this case, our default extrapolation model predicts that the firm will optimally delay default because overly optimistic investors pay high prices for bonds, keeping the cost of debt issuance low. However, the fundamental extrapolation model predicts that the firm will optimally accelerate default-by lowering the leverage threshold at which it defaults-because overly pessimistic bond investors make it more costly for the firm to issue debt. As a result, a model with fundamental extrapolation does not give rise to the "calm before the storm" phenomenon.

Instead, we would see light rain long before it pours. This alternative model would also not produce "default spirals." Although bond investors in this alternative model have biased beliefs about the growth rate of fundamentals, they would still price bonds using a full "structural" model of default. As in our fully rational benchmark, bond prices would rise following a default and the resulting restructuring. Specifically, bond investors would understand that restructuring raises v t above the default boundary, reducing future default risk and increasing post-restructuring bond prices.

We develop a model of credit cycles in which bond investors extrapolate past defaults. Our key contribution is to formalize reflexivity in credit markets, a dynamic two-way feedback loop between biased investor beliefs and credit market outcomes. This two-way feedback mechanism is particularly germane in credit markets because firms must return to the market to refinance maturing debt; the terms on which debt can be refinanced affect the likelihood of future defaults; and future default realizations, in turn, drive future investor beliefs. As we have shown, the combination of extrapolative beliefs and reflexive dynamics can lead to large short-run disconnects between cash flow fundamentals and credit market outcomes, including "calm before the storm" and "default spiral" episodes. Although optimistic investor beliefs tend to be partially self-fulfilling in short run, they are often self-defeating over longer horizons because they induce an endogenous rise in firm leverage and a buildup of financial fragility. Extrapolative beliefs also naturally lead to bond return predictability. But what is most striking here is that changes in investor sentiment can have an ambiguous impact on expected bond returns due to the reflexive nature of credit markets. When investors become more bullish, in the short run this can predict positive returns, even if expected returns become more negative over longer horizons. Our analysis leaves open at least three directions for future research. First, we have not allowed credit market conditions to explicitly affect firm investment or the underlying fundamentals of the economy. 33 However, as demonstrated by a growing macro-finance literature, the inability to access credit on reasonable terms following a credit market bust may exacerbate an incipient economic downturn. Indeed, López-Salido et al. (2017) and Mian et al. (2017) show that periods of credit market overheating forecast low economic growth. Incorporating these features into our model would likely further strengthen the feedback loop between investor sentiment and credit market outcomes. 34 Recent work by Maxted (2024), Krishnamurthy and Li (2025), and Bordalo, Gennaioli, Shleifer, and Terry (2026) has made progress in this direction.

Second, we have remained silent on welfare and optimal policy, even though our model suggests a potential role for policy intervention. During credit booms, elevated sentiment can temporarily prevent defaults, which can be welfare-improving if fundamentals recover soon enough. Nonetheless, self-fulfilling beliefs during default spirals can be welfare-reducing, both because these deteriorating beliefs accelerate future default realizations and because they lead to a slow recovery in the presence of improving fundamentals. Accepting these takeaways at face value, our model suggests a role for policy in moderating investor beliefs. Third, our model has implications for the literature on sovereign debt crises. Specifically, one could assume that a higher rate of current investment-which reduces current cash flows to equity holders-raises the growth rate of firm fundamentals (i.e., the growth rate of pretax operating cash flows). Unless the true risk of near-term default is very low, elevated bond investor sentiment would raise the optimal level of firm investment in this setting. How would introducing endogenous investment affect credit market dynamics in our model? High credit market sentiment would lead the firm to choose a higher rate of investment, raising subsequent fundamental growth and extending credit market booms.
